planting.note: Plant in deep, loose, well-drained sand on a sunny to lightly shaded upper slope, and withhold extra irrigation once roots are established.

directions: Apalachicola rosemary is endemic to a handful of sites in Liberty County, Florida, where it grows along the upper rims of steephead ravines as they transition into sandy longleaf pine sandhills. This aromatic, rosemary-scented mint relative wants sharply drained, deep sandy soil and full sun to light shade, and it is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once established, with overwatering being the most common cause of failure. It roots readily from softwood cuttings, which is how most nursery stock and conservation translocation plantings are produced. As a federally and state endangered species, source plants only from the small number of regional native nurseries that legally propagate it rather than wild-collected material.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Recovery Plan for Apalachicola Rosemary
